theory.title: How Packets Find Their Way
theory.plainObjective: Get your packet from Start to the Server by choosing the right path at router R1.
theory.summary: Every router on the internet does exactly this: looks up the destination IP in a table and picks an exit port. This decision happens billions of times per second, invisibly, for every message you send.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Why does a routing table exist?
bodyParagraphs.text: A router connects multiple networks. Without a routing table it has no idea which direction to send a packet - it would have to flood every port and let every connected device sort it out, which would overwhelm the network instantly. The routing table solves this: it is a lookup list that maps destination address ranges to specific exit ports, so the router can make a fast, precise forwarding decision for every packet.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Network interfaces - eth0, eth1...
bodyParagraphs.text: An interface is a physical (or virtual) port on the router - the socket where a cable plugs in. eth0 is the first Ethernet port, eth1 the second, and so on. Think of a router as a building with multiple doors: eth0 leads to one corridor, eth1 to another. The routing table is the sign at the entrance telling each visitor which door to use based on their destination.

bodyParagraphs.heading: CIDR notation: reading 192.168.1.0/24
bodyParagraphs.text:
The /24 is a prefix length. An IPv4 address has 32 bits, written as four groups of 0-255. /24 means the first 24 bits - the first three groups - are fixed and name the network. The remaining 8 bits identify a host inside it. So 192.168.1.0/24 covers every address from 192.168.1.0 to 192.168.1.255: 256 addresses whose first three groups are all 192.168.1.

A larger prefix number means a smaller, more specific network. /24 gives 256 addresses. /8 (like 10.0.0.0/8) fixes only the first group and covers over 16 million addresses. /32 fixes all 32 bits and means exactly one host.

To check if an IP matches a prefix, a router zeroes out the host bits and compares. 192.168.1.20 with 24 bits masked becomes 192.168.1.0 - a match. 10.0.0.5 masked to 24 bits becomes 10.0.0.0 - no match for 192.168.1.0/24.

bodyParagraphs.heading: A concrete example
bodyParagraphs.text: R1 in this level has two rows. Your destination is 192.168.1.20. Masking it against /24 gives 192.168.1.0, which matches the first row - so R1 sends you out eth0. If you were heading to 10.0.0.5 instead, masking against /8 gives 10.0.0.0, matching the second row, and you would leave via eth1 - a completely different physical path.

theory.mission:
You are 192.168.1.5 delivering to 192.168.1.20.

At R1: find the routing table row whose prefix covers 192.168.1.20, then move through that exit.

termIntroductions.headline: IP Address
termIntroductions.body: Your unique address on the network: 192.168.1.5. The server you're delivering to is at 192.168.1.20. Use arrow keys to move.

termIntroductions.headline: Routing Table
termIntroductions.body: Each row has a prefix like 192.168.1.0/24. The /24 means the first 24 bits are fixed - any address starting with 192.168.1 matches. Find the row whose prefix covers your destination 192.168.1.20 and take that exit.
